name: Ceftriaxone
route_note: Once-daily IV or IM injection; long half-life allows outpatient parenteral therapy.

discovery.note: Developed in the late 1970s; an aminothiazolyl methoxyimino side chain and a triazine-thiol group give broad Gram-negative activity and a long half-life. Year of first patent (1978), per Wikipedia.

tagline: Once-daily third-generation cephalosporin for meningitis, pneumonia and gonorrhoea
summary: Ceftriaxone is a broad-spectrum, once-daily injectable cephalosporin introduced by Roche in the early 1980s. It is a cornerstone treatment for bacterial meningitis, severe community-acquired pneumonia, gonorrhoea and many serious infections, and is one of the most used hospital antibiotics worldwide.
mechanism: Ceftriaxone binds penicillin-binding proteins (notably PBP3 in Gram-negative rods and PBP1/2 in streptococci), inhibiting cell-wall synthesis and causing bactericidal lysis.

Its oxyimino side chain makes it stable to many common beta-lactamases, but it is hydrolysed by extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs), AmpC enzymes and carbapenemases. It is highly protein-bound with partly biliary elimination, which explains its long half-life and biliary side effects.
uses: Complicated urinary tract, intra-abdominal (with metronidazole), bone and joint infections

history.title: Generics
history.detail: Patent expiry leads to many generic versions.

history.title: Calcium interaction warning
history.detail: FDA warns about fatal ceftriaxone–calcium precipitates in neonates' lungs and kidneys.

history.title: Gonorrhoea resistance
history.detail: The first reported cases of gonorrhoea with high-level azithromycin and ceftriaxone resistance (UK, Australia) raise alarm.

history.title: Single-agent gonorrhoea therapy
history.detail: CDC guidance moves to a single 500 mg IM dose of ceftriaxone for uncomplicated gonorrhoea.

facts: Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in hyperbilirubinaemic neonates because it displaces bilirubin from albumin.
It is classified in the WHO 'Watch' antibiotic group.
